notes.19.1: 'mille prope pugnas ... gladiatores imperator exhibuit': 'gladiatores' looks corrupt (perhaps for 'gladiatorias'); rendered 'gladiatorial fights'. 'eum longa aegritudine' read as 'cum'.

nodes.text: Some say, and it seems likely, that Commodus Antoninus, his successor and son, was not born of him but of adultery, and they weave a tale of this kind in common talk: that Faustina, daughter of Pius and wife of Marcus, having once seen gladiators pass by, was inflamed with love for one of them, and, suffering from a long illness, confessed the love to her husband. When Marcus referred this to the Chaldeans, their advice was that the gladiator should be killed and Faustina should bathe herself from below in his blood and then lie with her husband. When this was done, the love was indeed dissolved, but Commodus was born a gladiator, not an emperor; for as emperor he put on nearly a thousand gladiatorial fights in public, with the people looking on, as will be shown in his life. This is held to be likely from the fact that the son of so holy an emperor had such a character as no trainer of gladiators, no stage performer, no arena fighter had, no one, in short, compounded from the sewage of every disgrace and crime. But many report that Commodus was in any case born of adultery, since it is well established that Faustina, at Caieta, chose lovers for herself from among both sailors and gladiators. When Marcus Antoninus was told about her that he should divorce her, if he would not kill her, he is said to have said: 'If we send away the wife, let us return the dowry too.' And what was counted as the dowry? The empire, which he had received from his father-in-law, having been adopted at Hadrian's wish. So much, indeed, do the life, holiness, calm and piety of a good emperor prevail that no discredit attaching to anyone close to him tarnishes his fame. In short, to Antoninus, since he always kept to his own character and was not changed by anyone's whispering, a gladiator son and a disreputable wife did no harm; and he is held to be a god even now, as has always seemed and still seems right to you yourselves, most sacred Emperor Diocletian, who venerate him among your deities, not as you do the others but in a special way, and often say that you desire to be such in life and clemency as Marcus was, even though in philosophy not even Plato could be [his equal], were he to return to life. And these things [have been said] briefly and in a heap.
